newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada raises tobacco taxes, sets ad ban.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada raises tobacco taxes, sets ad ban.

text.p: Canada said on Thursday it would hike tobacco taxes, extend a surtax on tobacco makers' profits and ban tobacco advertising on television, radio and billboards as part of a sweeping new anti-tobacco strategy.

The government package, aimed at countering tobacco use, especially among youth, included a federal and provincial excise tax hike on cigarettes in Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, representing most of Canada's population.

Finance Minister Paul Martin said that at midnight Thursday excise taxes would increase by C$1.40 ($1.04) a carton of 200 cigarettes, split equally between the provinces and Ottawa. The federal portion would bring in C$75 million ($56 million) a year, the Finance Department said.
The three-year extension of the surtax on tobacco profits, which continued at a rate of 40 percent, would raise C$65 million Canadian ($48.2 million) per fiscal year, the government added.

Health Minister David Dingwall's sweeping advertising ban, responding in part to a Canadian Supreme Court decision in September 1995 that struck down a ban on tobacco ads on the grounds of freedom of speech, would allow tobacco ads in magazines and newspapers with primarily adult readership.
But the legislation, to be introduced in December, would ban sales of tobacco products through vending machines, self-service displays and mail-order sales.

"The need for action is clear. Seven million Canadians are currently victims of tobacco addiction," Dingwall told a news conference. "Tobacco will cause the deaths of more than 40,000 Canadians this year -- three times the number who will die from car accidents, suicides, drug abuse, murder and AIDS combined."

The proposed legislation, likely to pass since the Liberal government commands a solid majority in the House of Commons, would also restrict the use of tobacco brand names in sporting, music and other sponsored events.
But the tobacco companies would be allowed to put brand names on the bottom 10 percent of ads and direct mailings.
Manufacturers would be required to include additional information about the toxic substances in tobacco products and their health impacts on tobacco packaging.
Dingwall said an anti-smuggling plan introduced in 1994 would be extended.
The federal government cut tobacco taxes by C$5 ($4) a carton in 1994 to counteract widespread cigarette smuggling from the United States. It raised taxes by C$0.60 Canadian ($0.45) a carton in 1995.
Finance Minister Martin asserted that the government had "broken the backs of many organized tobacco smuggling rings in Canada."
The three major players in the Canadian tobacco market are:
- Imperial Tobacco Ltd, a unit of Imasco Ltd, which controls about 65 percent of the Canadian cigarette market. Imasco is 40 percent owned by B.A.T. Industries Plc of Britain.
- Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc, owned 60 percent by Rothmans International, a unit of Rothmans International Plc, and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos Inc.
- RJR MacDonald, wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
